Chapter Seven: The Cross and the Everyday Struggle.
Let’s be honest—life isn’t usually made of big, dramatic moments. Most days, it’s the little things that shape us. Maybe it’s a tense conversation over breakfast, the weight of a stack of bills, or just that quiet ache of feeling alone. Sometimes, it’s the slow disappointment that creeps in when things don’t go our way.
So, what does the message of the cross have to do with all of this? Well, it turns out, a lot. The cross isn’t just for the big crises. It speaks right into the routines and ruts of our ordinary days.
Think about those moments we all know too well—someone snaps at a loved one over something small, and then replays it in their mind all day, wishing they could just take it back. Or maybe you’ve felt invisible at work, wondering if what you do even matters. Here’s where the cross steps in—not with judgment, but with deep understanding.
Grace isn’t just for the big failures. It’s for the small ones, too.
A lot of us carry silent battles—maybe it’s insecurity, doubt, or that nagging fear that we’re just not enough. The cross never promises those struggles will vanish overnight. But it does offer a different perspective. It says, hey, your worth isn’t about how well you perform, or how flawless your record is. Even on your worst days, you’re still loved.
And that changes everything, doesn’t it? Instead of hustling for approval, you can actually rest in acceptance.
The stories in this book bring that to life. Picture a parent who, after years of losing patience, finally finds the freedom to apologize, and start fresh. Or a worker who stops chasing recognition and starts finding real meaning in quietly serving others. These aren’t overnight transformations. They’re slow, steady shifts—a new way of living that grows from the inside out.
The cross becomes like a lens, changing how we see every moment, even the most mundane. It invites us to bring our whole selves—failures, fears, and all—and discover that, yes, grace really is enough.
So, here’s the key: it’s not about escaping the everyday struggle. It’s about finding hope, and even purpose, right in the middle of it.
